If a second triage test or follow-up test was conducted as part of the screening strategy, the individual should still only be counted once. Disaggregation of data should include: Age groups (15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–49, 50+ years). Number of lifetime screening tests (e.g., first in lifetime, second in lifetime, etc.). Geographic and administrative areas of epidemiological importance. Core Indicator: Percentage of women living with HIV who screened positive for pre-invasive cervical disease and received treatment. What it measures: This indicator evaluates progress toward achieving the treatment coverage target of 90% of women with a positive screening test receiving treatment, as outlined in the Global Strategy for cervical cancer elimination. Rationale: This indicator assesses the availability, accessibility, and coverage of treatment for pre-invasive cervical disease among women living with HIV who were diagnosed with precancerous lesions during screening and were eligible for treatment, in alignment with WHO recommendations for cervical cancer prevention. The WHO Global Strategy aims to eliminate cervical cancer by achieving the following targets by 2030: vaccinating 90% of eligible girls against HPV, screening 70% of eligible women at least twice in their lifetimes, and effectively treating 90% of those with a positive screening test or cervical lesion, including palliative care when necessary. Numerator: The number of women living with HIV who received treatment after screening positive for pre-invasive cervical disease and were deemed eligible for treatment according to WHO recommendations. Denominator: The number of women living with HIV who screened positive for pre-invasive cervical disease. Method of measurement: Data should be derived from health facility patient registers and patient records. Treatment options include thermal ablation, cryotherapy, and excision treatments such as Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ). Core Indicator: Percentage of women living with HIV diagnosed with invasive cervical cancer who were treated. What it measures: This indicator tracks progress in increasing access to treatment for invasive cervical cancer among women living with HIV. Rationale: The purpose of this indicator is to monitor trends in the availability and accessibility of treatment services for invasive cervical cancer among women living with HIV. Over time, the number of women living with HIV receiving treatment for invasive cervical cancer is expected to plateau and gradually decrease as screening programs expand, enabling earlier detection and treatment of precancerous lesions, and as HPV vaccination coverage increases in line with the WHO Global Strategy's 90–70–90 elimination targets. Numerator: The number of women living with HIV who received treatment after being diagnosed with invasive cervical cancer. Denominator: The number of women living with HIV who were diagnosed with invasive cervical cancer. Method of measurement: This data is generated from programmatic records from HIV or cervical cancer programs, or from national cancer registries where HIV status is recorded. Disaggregation of data should include: Age groups (15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–49, 50+ years). Episodes of invasive cervical cancer treatment (e.g., first in lifetime, second, third, etc.). Core Indicator: Crude probability of surviving one year after a diagnosis of cervical cancer. What it measures: This indicator evaluates the effectiveness of cervical cancer treatment for women diagnosed with cervical cancer. Rationale: Monitoring cervical cancer survival among women living with HIV is essential for assessing access to and effectiveness of treatment and follow-up care to support the needs of cancer survivors. Adequate and complete follow-up is a prerequisite for conducting a survival study. This indicator is calculated by assessing the percentage of women living with HIV who were diagnosed with invasive cervical cancer and were still alive 12 months after their diagnosis. It excludes those who were not followed for the 12-month period. In settings with good retention and follow-up, five-year survival can also be calculated, including only individuals under observation with complete follow-up five years after their cervical cancer diagnosis. Numerator: The number of women living with HIV who are still alive 12 months after receiving a diagnosis of invasive cervical cancer. Denominator: The number of women living with HIV who received a diagnosis of invasive cervical cancer within a 12-month cohort observation period. Method of measurement: This indicator uses cohort analysis to measure the proportion of women living with HIV who are still alive 12 months after their cervical cancer diagnosis. Data sources include individual-level data obtained from program records. Core Indicator: Estimated number of people newly infected with HIV per 1,000 uninfected population. What it measures: This indicator tracks progress toward ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic and achieving the goal of zero new infections. Rationale: The overarching goal of the global HIV/AIDS response is to reduce the number of new infections to fewer than 200,000 by 2030. Numerator: The number of people newly infected with HIV during the reporting period. Denominator: The total number of uninfected individuals (or person-years exposed). Method of measurement: This can be measured using individual-level program data or mathematical modeling tools such as Spectrum AIM, which incorporate data from geographical and population-specific surveys, surveillance data (e.g., case reporting, mortality, program, and clinical data), and assumptions about HIV transmission. Disaggregation of data should include: Gender (female, male, other). Age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49, 50+ years). Probable route of transmission (e.g., heterosexual sex, sex between men, unprotected intercourse during sex work, injecting drug use with unsterile equipment, nosocomial, vertical, other). Key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people living in prisons or other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender and gender-diverse individuals, adolescent girls, and young women). Core Indicator: Percentage of key population members who avoid health care due to stigma and discrimination. What it measures: This indicator evaluates the extent to which perceived stigma and discrimination in health care settings lead members of key populations to avoid seeking health care. Rationale: Health care settings are among the most common places where members of key populations experience discrimination. Tracking the proportion of key populations avoiding health care due to stigma and discrimination provides managers with information on where to focus efforts to reduce discrimination and perceived discrimination by service providers, as well as identifying areas where service utilization by key populations can be improved. Numerator: The number of survey respondents from key populations who answer yes to any of the following: Have you ever avoided seeking: Any health care? HIV testing? HIV medical care? HIV treatment? In the last 12 months, due to any of the following: Fear of or concern about stigma. Fear or concern that someone may learn you are a member of a key population. Fear of or concern about or experience of violence. Fear of or concern about or experience of harassment or arrest by police. Denominator: The total number of survey respondents from key populations. Method of measurement: Representative surveys of key populations (e.g., Behavioral and Biological Surveillance [BBS], Behavioral Surveillance Surveys [BSS], HIV Sentinel Surveillance Plus [HSS+]). Recommended measurement periodicity is every 2–3 years.
